'''Barbara Ann Maher''' {{post-nominals|FRS}} is [[Professor]] Emerita of [[Environmental Science]] at [[Lancaster University]]. She served as director of the Centre for [[Environmental magnetism]] & [[Palaeomagnetism]]<ref name=gs>{{Google scholar id}}</ref> until 2021 and works on [[magnetic nanoparticle]]s and [[pollution]].<ref name=orcid>{{ORCID}}</ref>

== Education and early career ==
Maher earned her [[Bachelor's degree]] in [[geography]] at the [[University of Liverpool]]. She remained there for her graduate studies, earning a [[PhD]] in environmental [[geophysics]] for research on the origins and transformations of [[Magnetic mineralogy|magnetic minerals]] in [[soil]]s.<ref name=phd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|oclc=499883188|publisher=University of Liverpool|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.354553}}|url=https://copac.jisc.ac.uk/id/10802445?style=html|title=Origins and transformations of magnetic minerals in soils|first=Barbara Ann|last=Maher|year=1984|website=copac.jisc.ac.uk|accessdate=2019-01-29|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130000020/https://copac.jisc.ac.uk/id/10802445?style=html|archivedate=2019-01-30|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Career and research==
After completing her PhD, Maher was made a [[Natural Environment Research Council]] (NERC) [[Fellow]] at the [[Department of Geophysics, University of Edinburgh]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.lancaster.ac.uk/staff/maherb/|title=Prof. Barbara A Maher|last=|first=|date=|website=lancaster.ac.uk|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref> She joined the [[School of Environmental Sciences, University of East Anglia]] as a lecturer in 1987 and was promoted to Senior Lecturer in 1996 and Reader in 1998.<ref name=":0" /> Here she investigated the magnetic properties of ultrafine sub-micron [[magnetite]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Maher|first=Barbara A.|date=1988|title=Magnetic properties of some synthetic sub-micron magnetites|journal=Geophysical Journal International|volume=94|issue=1|pages=83–96|doi=10.1111/j.1365-246X.1988.tb03429.x|issn=0956-540X|bibcode=1988GeoJI..94...83M|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Maher|first1=Barbara A.|last2=Taylor|first2=Reginald M.|s2cid=4338921|date=1988|title=Formation of ultrafine-grained magnetite in soils|journal=Nature|volume=336|issue=6197|pages=368–370|doi=10.1038/336368a0|issn=1476-4687|bibcode=1988Natur.336..368M}} {{closed access}}</ref> Using her understanding of magnetic mineral formation in soils, she evaluated the paleo-climate of the [[Chinese Loess Plateau]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Maher|first1=Barbara A.|last2=Thompson|first2=Roy|date=1991|title=Mineral magnetic record of the Chinese loess and paleosols |journal=Geology|volume=19|issue=1|pages=3–6|doi=10.1130/0091-7613(1991)019<0003:MMROTC>2.3.CO;2|issn=0091-7613|bibcode=1991Geo....19....3M}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Maher|first=Barbara A.|date=1998|title=Magnetic properties of modern soils and Quaternary loessic paleosols: paleoclimatic implications|journal=Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology|volume=137|issue=1|pages=25–54|doi=10.1016/S0031-0182(97)00103-X|issn=0031-0182|bibcode=1998PPP...137...25M}}</ref> She developed spatial and temporal reconstructions of the Asian palaeo[[monsoon]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Maher|first1=B. A.|last2=Thompson|first2=R.|last3=Zhou|first3=L. P.|date=1994|title=Spatial and temporal reconstructions of changes in the Asian palaeomonsoon: A new mineral magnetic approach|journal=Earth and Planetary Science Letters|volume=125|issue=1|pages=461–471|doi=10.1016/0012-821X(94)90232-1|issn=0012-821X|bibcode=1994E&PSL.125..461M}}</ref> She was the [[Royal Institution]] ''Scientists for the new century'' lecturer in 1999.<ref name=":0" /> She edited the book ''Quaternary Climates, Environments and Magnetism'' in 1999.<ref>{{Cite book|date=1999|editor-last=Maher|editor-first=Barbara A.|editor2-last=Thompson|editor2-first=Roy|title=Quaternary Climates, Environments and Magnetism|doi=10.1017/cbo9780511535635|isbn=9780521624176}}</ref>

Maher also studies [[magnetic nanoparticles]] to track dust impacts on [[Climate change (general concept)|climate change]] and changes in human health due to particulate air pollution.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/barbara-maher-7562/|website=royalsociety.org|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20190129150658/https://royalsociety.org/people/barbara-maher-7562/|archivedate=2019-01-29|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|location=London|author=Anon|year=2006|title=Professor Barbara Maher: Research Fellow}}</ref> She was described by Richard Harrison as having "single-handedly developed the field of environmental magnetism".<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://www.lancaster.ac.uk/lec/news-and-events/news/2013/december/barbara-maher-medal/|title="Outstanding scientist" wins medal|last=University|first=Lancaster|date=|website=lancaster.ac.uk|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref> She demonstrated that soils that were exposed to higher rainfall make more [[magnetite]].<ref name=":1" /> She has studied how windblown dusts impacted the levels of [[greenhouse gas]]es.<ref name=":1" /> She is interested in magnetic records of [[Quaternary]] terrestrial sediments.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.research.lancs.ac.uk/portal/en/people/barbara-maher(bac8c1ef-a7ee-453b-9637-bed2931eb5ae).html|title=Barbara Maher - Research Portal {{!}} Lancaster University|website=research.lancs.ac.uk|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref> She launched the Quantifying Uncertainty in the Earth System (QUEST) Working Group on Dust in 2008.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bridge.bris.ac.uk/projects/dust|title=Home|website=bridge.bris.ac.uk|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref>

Maher became interested in metal-rich particulate pollution.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Maher|first1=B. A.|last2=Moore|first2=C.|last3=Matzka|first3=J.|date=2008|title=Spatial variation in vehicle-derived metal pollution identified by magnetic and elemental analysis of roadside tree leaves|journal=Atmospheric Environment|volume=42|issue=2|pages=364–373|doi=10.1016/j.atmosenv.2007.09.013|issn=1352-2310|bibcode=2008AtmEn..42..364M|url=https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/23605/1/Maher_Moore_Matzka_Atmos_Env_2007.pdf}}</ref> In 2013 Maher demonstrated that [[Silver Birch|silver birch]] trees could be used as pollution filters.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/articles/1m0KylS04ZqwcswP5Q8MQQq/the-big-air-pollution-experiment|title=BBC Two - Trust Me, I'm a Doctor, Series 1 - The big air pollution experiment|website=BBC|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iflscience.com/environment/trees-trap-environmental-particulate-matter/|title=Trees Trap Environmental Particulate Matter|website=IFLScience|date=26 November 2013 |access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref> The result was part of an investigation into the impact of roadside trees on the concentration of particulate matter found in people's homes.<ref name="MaherAhmed2013">{{cite journal|last1=Maher|first1=Barbara A.|last2=Ahmed|first2=Imad A. M.|last3=Davison|first3=Brian|last4=Karloukovski|first4=Vassil|last5=Clarke|first5=Robert|title=Impact of Roadside Tree Lines on Indoor Concentrations of Traffic-Derived Particulate Matter|journal=Environmental Science & Technology|volume=47|issue=23|year=2013|pages=13737–13744|issn=0013-936X|doi=10.1021/es404363m|pmid=24215538|bibcode=2013EnST...4713737M}}</ref> Silver birch trees are covered in tiny hairs, which can trap the particulate matter whilst allowing clean air to circulate.<ref name=":3" /> The matter is washed off the leaves when it rains, allowing the birch trees to trap even more particulate matter.<ref name=":3" /> Her work was examined by [[Michael Mosley]] and [[Gabriel Weston]] on the [[BBC]] show ''[[Trust Me, I'm a Doctor (TV series)|Trust Me, I'm a Doctor]]''.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.lancaster.ac.uk/news/articles/2013/professor-on-bbc-tv-health-programme/|title=Professor on BBC TV health programme {{!}} Lancaster University|last=University|first=Lancaster|website=lancaster.ac.uk|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref> They found that the pollution collected in houses protected by silver birch trees was 50 - 60% lower than in houses without them.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://plantsatwork.org.uk/index.php/all-news/item/trust-me-i-m-a-doctor-plants-clean-up|title=PlantsAtWork.org.uk - Trust Me I'm a Doctor: plants clean up|website=plantsatwork.org.uk|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/article/tree-of-life-birch-filters-out-deadly-diesel-pollution-gcgsrmwcjkw|title=Tree of life: birch filters out deadly diesel pollution|last=Summers|first=Hannah|date=2013-10-20|website=[[The Times]]|publisher=The Sunday Times|access-date=2019-01-19|issn=0956-1382}} {{subscription required}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.monmouthshirebeacon.co.uk/article.cfm?id=383&headline=Silver%20birches%20the%20answer%20to%20%20pollution?&searchyear=2014|title=Silver birches the answer to pollution?|website=Monmouthshire Beacon|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref>

In 2016 Maher found toxic, metal-rich nanoparticles in human [[brain tissue]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2016/sep/05/toxic-air-pollution-particles-found-in-human-brains-links-alzheimers|title=Toxic air pollution particles found in human brains|last=Carrington|first=Damian|date=2016-09-05|website=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=2019-01-19|issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.lancaster.ac.uk/news/articles/2016/toxic-air-pollution-nanoparticles-discovered-in-the-human-brain/|title=Toxic air pollution nanoparticles discovered in the human brain {{!}} Lancaster University|last=University|first=Lancaster|website=lancaster.ac.uk|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2016/09/06/health/air-pollution-inside-the-brain/index.html|title=Air pollution particles found inside human brains|author=Meera Senthilingam|website=CNN|date=6 September 2016 |access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iflscience.com/brain/magnetite-in-the-brain-probably-comes-from-air-pollution/|title=Magnetite In the Brain Probably Comes From Air Pollution|website=IFLScience|date=5 September 2016 |access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref> By studying the nanoparticles using an [[electron microscope]], Maher found they were small and round, some with surface crystallites, indicating that they had been formed at high temperatures, rather than in the brain itself.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/chemicals-linked-to-health-hazards-are-common-in-household-dust/|title=Chemicals Linked to Health Hazards Are Common in Household Dust|last=Skwarecki|first=Beth|website=scientificamerican.com|publisher=[[Scientific American]]|year=2016|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref> The nanoparticles comprise a mix of iron-rich, strongly magnetic particles associated with other metals, including platinum, cobalt, aluminium and titanium. Similar metal-rich nanoparticles occur in abundance in urban air pollution, especially at busy roadsides. As the nanoparticles have diameters that are less than 200&nbsp;nm, they can enter the brain via the lungs and blood circulation, via ingestion and transport through the neuroenteric system, and through the [[olfactory nerve]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Maher |first1=Barbara A. |last2=Ahmed |first2=Imad A. M. |last3=Karloukovski |first3=Vassil |last4=MacLaren |first4=David A. |last5=Foulds |first5=Penelope G. |last6=Allsop |first6=David |last7=Mann |first7=David M. A. |last8=Torres-Jardon |first8=Ricardo |last9=Calderon-Garciduenas |first9=Lilian |date=2016 |title=Magnetite pollution nanoparticles in the human brain |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=113 |issue=39 |pages=10797–10801 |bibcode=2016PNAS..11310797M |doi=10.1073/pnas.1605941113 |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=5047173 |pmid=27601646 |doi-access=free}}</ref> [[Magnetite]] can produce [[reactive oxygen species]] in the brain.<ref name=":4" /> Maher became concerned that these [[magnetite]] particles could be linked to [[Alzheimer's disease]], [[mental illness]] and reduced intelligence.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2016/09/05/air-pollution-particles-linked-to-alzheimers-found-in-human-brai/|title='Air pollution' particles linked to Alzheimer's found in human brain|last=Knapton|first=Sarah|date=2016-09-05|newspaper=The Telegraph|access-date=2019-01-19|issn=0307-1235}}</ref> Her work on air pollution nanoparticles in human tissues attracts worldwide scientific, and media, attention. She has appeared on numerous BBC News and World Service TV and radio programmes, including [[BBC Radio 4]]'s ''[[Inside Science]]'' in 2018, discussing the [[Government of the United Kingdom]] Clean Air Strategy.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/m00021r4|title=BBC Radio 4 - BBC Inside Science, Clean Air Strategy, Fast Radio Bursts and Kuba Kingdom|website=BBC|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref> 

== Awards and honours ==
*1999 [[Royal Institution]] Lecturer, Scientists for the New Century
*2005 Chree Medal and Prize, [[Institute of Physics]] (IOP), renamed [[Institute of Physics Edward Appleton Medal and Prize]] in 2008<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.iop.org/about/awards/subject/appleton/medallists/page_38521.html|title=Appleton medal recipients|website=iop.org|access-date=2019-01-19|archive-date=16 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170816021708/http://www.iop.org/about/awards/subject/appleton/medallists/page_38521.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
*2002-2006 and 2006-2008 Chair, Rock Magnetism group, International Union of Geophysics & Geodesy
*2006-2012 [[Royal Society Wolfson Research Merit Award]]<ref name=":1" />
*2008 -2010 Vice President of the ''[[Quaternary Research]]'' Association<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.qra.org.uk/uploads/documents/CircularFeb09.pdf|title=QRA Executive Committee 2009|last=|first=|date=|website=QRA|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref>
*2013 Pilkington Teaching Award, [[Lancaster University]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.lancaster.ac.uk/lec/about-us/people/barbara-maher|title=Barbara Maher|website=lancaster.ac.uk|access-date=2019-01-19}}</ref>
*2014 Schlumberger Medal and Award, [[Mineralogical Society of Great Britain and Ireland]], renamed the Neumann Medal in 2021 <ref name=":2" />
*2020 Fellowship, [[American Geophysical Union]]<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|title=Lancaster Scientist lauded for 'exceptional contribution' to Earth sciences|url=https://www.lancaster.ac.uk/lec/about-us/news/lancaster-scientist-lauded-for-exceptional-contribution-to-earth-sciences|access-date=2021-06-27|website=www.lancaster.ac.uk|language=en}}</ref>
*2021 Bullard Lecturer, [[American Geophysical Union]]<ref name=":5" />
*2023 AGU College of Fellows Distinguished Lecturer
*2024 Awarded membership, Academia Europaea
*2024 Elected, [[Fellow of the Royal Society]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor Barbara Maher FRS |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/barbara-maher-36743/ |access-date=2024-05-20 |website=Royal Society |language=en}}</ref>
